text:
[
  {
    "n": 1,
    "title": "Epistemology and the Definition of Knowledge",
    "scope": "This part establishes the philosophical foundations of artificial intelligence by defining knowledge through classical epistemology. It introduces the tripartite definition of knowledge as Justified True Belief (JTB) traced to Socrates, breaking down the distinct roles of objective truth, subjective belief, and justification. It then explores Edmund Gettier's 1963 challenge demonstrating that JTB is insufficient when justification is only accidentally connected to truth.",
    "key_points": [
      "Etymology: epistemology derives from Greek episteme (knowledge) and logos (logical discourse/study)",
      "Tripartite definition of knowledge (JTB): Truth (objective reality), Belief (subjective representation of reality), and Justification (explanatory grounding)",
      "Socrates' formulation: Knowledge is Justified True Belief",
      "Gettier counterexample (1963): Smith and Jones applying for a job; the ten coins in the pocket; justified belief accidentally coinciding with truth",
      "Epistemological lesson: Justification must be non-accidentally and properly connected to the truth to count as genuine knowledge"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 2,
    "title": "The Turing Test and Operational Intelligence",
    "scope": "This part examines Alan Turing's operational redefinition of intelligence and the historical emergence of AI philosophy. It introduces the 1950 Mind paper 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' and the Imitation Game setup. It also covers the inverse Turing test implemented in CAPTCHA systems to differentiate humans from automated agents.",
    "key_points": [
      "Alan Turing's foundational contributions: Universal Turing Machine, Church-Turing thesis, Bletchley Park Bombe decoder, and 1950 Mind paper",
      "Reframing the question: replacing 'Can machines think?' with behavioral indistinguishability ('Can a machine behave so that an interrogator cannot distinguish it from a human?')",
      "The Imitation Game protocol: human interrogator communicating via text/teletype with a hidden human and a hidden machine",
      "Domain limitations of the Turing Test and historical milestone benchmarks",
      "The Inverse Turing Test: CAPTCHA (Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart) via distorted text (reCAPTCHA/OCR), audio, and image-grid classification"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 3,
    "title": "Syntax, Semantics, and the Chinese Room Argument",
    "scope": "This part examines the internal limitations of symbolic and behavioral AI through John Searle's 1980 Chinese Room thought experiment. It details the fundamental distinction between syntax (formal symbol manipulation) and semantics (conceptual meaning and intentionality). It presents counterarguments to Searle, such as the Systems Reply and machine rule induction, alongside the cognitive pipeline of computer perception.",
    "key_points": [
      "John Searle's 1980 thought experiment: English speaker locked in a room manipulating Chinese characters using a rulebook and input/output slots",
      "Critique of Strong AI and the Turing Test: passing a behavioral test does not entail mental states or linguistic understanding",
      "Syntax vs. Semantics distinction: computers operate purely on symbolic form and grammatical rules (syntax) without grasping intrinsic meaning (semantics)",
      "Counters to the Chinese Room: Systems Reply (the room as a whole understands), external grounding, and machine learning/rule induction from data",
      "Computer perception vs. human conceptualization: the 4-stage pipeline (segmentation, detection, conceptualization, verbalization) applied to varied instances of a concept (e.g., 'chair')"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 4,
    "title": "Robot Ethics and Asimov's Laws",
    "scope": "This part explores normative ethics and autonomous safety through Isaac Asimov's Laws of Robotics and modern autonomous systems. It presents the hierarchical structure of the original Three Laws and the later Zeroth Law. It then bridges science fiction to real-world engineering dilemmas, including physical workspace safety envelopes, military lethal autonomous weapons, and municipal police robotics.",
    "key_points": [
      "Asimov's First Law: A robot may not injure a human being or, through inaction, allow a human being to come to harm",
      "Asimov's Second Law: A robot must obey human orders, except where such orders conflict with the First Law",
      "Asimov's Third Law: A robot must protect its own existence, provided this does not conflict with the First or Second Law",
      "The Zeroth Law: A robot may not injure humanity or, through inaction, allow humanity to come to harm, introducing utilitarian ethical calculus",
      "Modern physical robot safety: industrial caged cells, safety mats, light curtains, muting sensors, and collaborative robotics (cobots)",
      "Lethal robotics and legal frameworks: international law, constitutional use-of-force standards, semi-autonomous combat drones, and armed tactical robots (e.g., Dallas 2016)"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 5,
    "title": "Propositional Logic: Propositions, Connectives, and Truth Tables",
    "scope": "This part introduces formal symbolic reasoning starting from propositional logic. It defines what constitutes a valid proposition in classical bivalent logic versus commands, questions, and open formulas. It teaches truth assignments, truth table mechanics for 2^n cases, and all standard binary and unary logical operators.",
    "key_points": [
      "Definition of a proposition: a declarative statement that is strictly either true (T) or false (F), but not both",
      "Non-propositions: imperative commands ('Open the window'), interrogatives ('Is the server running?'), and open expressions with free variables ('x + 3 = 5')",
      "Atomic propositions vs. compound propositions formed via logical connectives",
      "Standard operators: Negation (\\neg), Conjunction (\\land), Disjunction (\\lor), Conditional (\\to), Biconditional (\\leftrightarrow)",
      "Inclusive OR vs. Exclusive OR (\\oplus): truth condition comparison",
      "Material implication (p \\to q): truth table, false antecedent yielding true ('vacuous truth'), and English mappings ('q if p', 'p only if q')",
      "Systematic truth table construction: 2^n rows for n distinct propositional variables"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 6,
    "title": "Propositional Reasoning: Equivalences, Conditional Forms, and Satisfiability",
    "scope": "This part covers semantic properties of propositional formulas and formal methods for establishing equivalence without building full truth tables. It introduces the classification of formulas into tautologies, contradictions, and contingencies, alongside satisfiability. It defines conditional transformations (converse, inverse, contrapositive) and algebraic equivalence laws.",
    "key_points": [
      "Formula classification: Tautology (true under every assignment), Contradiction (false under every assignment), Contingency (true under some, false under others)",
      "Satisfiability: a formula is satisfiable iff at least one model/assignment makes it true (tautologies and contingencies are satisfiable; contradictions are unsatisfiable)",
      "Conditional variants: Converse (q \\to p), Inverse (\\neg p \\to \\neg q), Contrapositive (\\neg q \\to \\neg p)",
      "Equivalence of contrapositive: p \\to q \\equiv \\neg q \\to \\neg p",
      "Core equivalence laws: Double negation (\\neg\\neg p \\equiv p), De Morgan's laws (\\neg(p \\land q) \\equiv \\neg p \\lor \\neg q, \\neg(p \\lor q) \\equiv \\neg p \\land \\neg q)",
      "Implication identity (p \\to q \\equiv \\neg p \\lor q) and negated implication (\\neg(p \\to q) \\equiv p \\land \\neg q)",
      "Biconditional expansion: p \\leftrightarrow q \\equiv (p \\to q) \\land (q \\to p)",
      "Algebraic proofs of equivalence (e.g., proving p \\to (q \\lor r) \\equiv (p \\to q) \\lor (p \\to r) \\equiv \\neg p \\lor q \\lor r)"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 7,
    "title": "First-Order Logic: Syntax, Ontology, and Components",
    "scope": "This part motivates and defines First-Order Logic (FOL) as an expressive language overcoming the representational bottleneck of propositional logic. It introduces the full syntax and ontology of FOL, explaining domains, constants, variables, predicates, functions, and equality. It teaches the distinction between terms, atomic formulas, complex formulas, free vs. bound variables, and sentences.",
    "key_points": [
      "Limitations of propositional logic: inability to access internal object structures, shared properties, or quantify over sets of entities",
      "FOL ontological building blocks: Domain of discourse, Constants (names for specific entities, e.g., Ana), Variables (placeholders, e.g., x, y)",
      "Predicates: unary properties (e.g., Student(x)) and n-ary relations (e.g., Knows(x, y), Borders(x, y)) mapping terms to truth values",
      "Functions: mappings from domain elements to a unique domain element (e.g., mentorOf(x))",
      "Terms vs. Formulas: terms refer to objects (constants, variables, functions); formulas evaluate to truth values",
      "Atomic formulas: applying predicates to terms (P(t1, ..., tn)) or equating terms (t1 = t2)",
      "Variable binding and scope: free variables vs. bound variables; definition of an FOL sentence (a well-formed formula with no free variables)"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 8,
    "title": "Quantification, Negation, and Natural Language Translation in FOL",
    "scope": "This part details universal and existential quantifiers, their semantic interpretation over domains, and quantifier interaction rules. It covers quantifier ordering and scope alternation, De Morgan's quantifier duality laws, and formal natural language translation patterns into FOL expressions.",
    "key_points": [
      "Universal quantifier (\\forall x P(x)): 'P(x) holds for every object x in the domain'",
      "Existential quantifier (\\exists x P(x)): 'P(x) holds for at least one object x in the domain'",
      "Quantifier order sensitivity: \\forall x \\exists y Likes(x, y) ('Everyone likes someone') vs. \\exists y \\forall x Likes(x, y) ('There is someone whom everyone likes')",
      "Quantifier negation laws (duality): \\neg \\forall x P(x) \\equiv \\exists x \\neg P(x) and \\neg \\exists x P(x) \\equiv \\forall x \\neg P(x)",
      "Canonical translation patterns: universal quantification typically pairs with material implication (\\forall x (P(x) \\to Q(x))); existential quantification typically pairs with conjunction (\\exists x (P(x) \\land Q(x)))",
      "Complex relational translations: multi-variable constraints, border relationships, and formalizing uniqueness/exact quantification in FOL"
    ]
  }
]
